verses.text: The lot came out for the children of Joseph from the Jordan at Jericho, at the waters of Jericho on the east, even the wilderness, going up from Jericho through the hill country to Bethel.
It went out from Bethel to Luz, and passed along to the border of the Archites to Ataroth;
and it went down westward to the border of the Japhletites, to the border of Beth Horon the lower, and on to Gezer; and ended at the sea.
The children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance.
This was the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families. The border of their inheritance eastward was Ataroth Addar, to Beth Horon the upper.
The border went out westward at Michmethath on the north. The border turned about eastward to Taanath Shiloh, and passed along it on the east of Janoah.
It went down from Janoah to Ataroth, to Naarah, reached to Jericho, and went out at the Jordan.
From Tappuah the border went along westward to the brook of Kanah; and ended at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim according to their families;
together with the cities which were set apart for the children of Ephraim in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages.
They didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer; but the Canaanites dwell in the territory of Ephraim to this day, and have become servants to do forced labor.

footnotes.content: The children of Joseph—now split into two tribes—receive their inheritance by lot, just as the Lord promised. Notice how the land is measured precisely from the wilderness up through Bethel, a place where Jacob once wrestled with the Lord himself. Every boundary honored matters to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Bethel to Luz—the passage names both the old and new names of the same place, reminding us that God had already changed it when He appeared to Jacob. Even in land distribution, Scripture honors the memory of how the Lord had worked beforehand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The borders descend westward to the sea—down to Gezer, a place that will soon face a reckoning in verse 10. The Lord marks out the land generously, yet history shows not everything handed to us stays unmolested without our faithful obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The two brothers, Manasseh and Ephraim—descended from Joseph's own sons, adopted by Jacob at his deathbed—now possess the land together. What began as family tension and separation in Egypt now becomes shared inheritance, a taste of reconciliation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephraim's boundary is traced out precisely—Ataroth Addar to Beth Horon—written down so that no confusion would blur the line between siblings. The Lord's Word speaks clearly so His people need not quarrel over what is theirs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The border turns about eastward, winding through Taanath Shiloh and Janoah—names that mark a geography now sacred because it's where God's people will dwell. Every landmark here speaks of the Lord's faithfulness to bring them home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The boundary descends from Janoah back down to Jericho and the Jordan—full circle, back to where they crossed. The Lord does not give piecemeal or forgotten: the whole path is remembered, the whole inheritance secured.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inheritance of Ephraim is sealed—westward to the brook of Kanah, ending at the sea. These were the cities with their villages, a complete portion. The Lord does not measure stingily with those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even within the larger inheritance, Ephraim received cities set apart, cradled within Manasseh's territory—additional gifts, a sign of double honor to Joseph's legacy. The Lord's provisions often overflow in unexpected places for those He loves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: Ephraim did not drive out Gezer, and the Canaanites remained there, doing forced labor. What looked like mercy—letting them serve—was really a failure to claim the fullness of what the Lord gave. How often do we settle for partial obedience and tell ourselves it's enough?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
